verses.translation_literal: A psalm of Asaph. God has taken his stand in the assembly of El; in the midst of gods he judges.
verses.translation_dramatic: A psalm of Asaph. Hush. God has risen and taken his stand in the great assembly of El. In the very midst of the gods he sits in judgment.
verses.directors_commentary:
Stage this as a courtroom, not a sermon. 'Elohim' is used here three times in one breath: once with a singular verb (God, who has taken his stand) and once with plural sense (the gods, in whose midst he judges). The KJV 'the congregation of the mighty' blurs the second 'el into a bare adjective and so hides that the Hebrew has God standing in the assembly of El, a phrase that echoes the old Canaanite picture of a divine council presided over by El, with the lesser gods beneath him. The psalm borrows that picture, but with a twist: here the council does not meet to receive orders, it is on trial. The verb 'nitzav', 'stationed, standing', is the posture of one who rises to deliver a verdict or to prosecute; in a Near Eastern court the judge usually sits, so a judge who stands is a judge about to act. Note that the Hebrew verse numbering counts the superscription as part of verse 1, which is why the KJV prints it as 82:0.

The traditional commentators mostly read the second 'elohim' as human judges, as the word can mean in Exodus 21:6 and 22:8 (Rashi, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David, Malbim, who ties the psalm to Jehoshaphat's appointing of judges in 2 Chronicles 19). Ibn Ezra reads them as angels. The actors need not settle this; they need only play that the beings in the room think themselves untouchable, and that God is not afraid of them.

philological_notes.note: Niphal participle: 'is stationed, standing'. It describes a standing already taken up, and in legal scenes a standing to deliver judgment (compare Isa 3:13, where God 'stands to contend'). The plain 'is standing' is richer than the KJV 'standeth'.

'adah is a gathering, an assembly; the same word is used of the congregation of Israel, but here it is the assembly of El. Ibn Ezra takes it as the glory dwelling with the congregation of Israel; the plain sense is the heavenly council.
The verb 'shaphat' covers the whole work of a ruler-judge: to hear, decide, and rule. It returns in vv. 2, 3 and 8, and is the thread of the psalm.

verses.translation_literal: Until when will you judge injustice, and the faces of the wicked will you lift up? Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: How long? How long will you give judgment that is no judgment at all, and lift the faces of the wicked and honor them? Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the indictment, and it begins with a groan rather than a charge: 'ad-matai', 'until when?', the cry of the oppressed turned on the oppressors. Play it as weary, not shouted. The KJV 'accept the persons of the wicked' is an archaism that now sounds like 'admit them'. The Hebrew idiom is 'to lift the face', which means to show favor, to treat someone as important: a judge who lifts a man's face will not look him in the eye as an equal but raises him in rank. That is favoritism (compare Lev 19:15, which forbids lifting the face of the poor as well as honoring the face of the great). 'Avel', 'injustice', is literally what is crooked, a judgment off the true line. Note the addressees are plural ('you will judge'): the speaker is God, the accused are the gods.

'Selah' is a liturgical marker whose meaning is uncertain, perhaps a pause, a musical lift, or a lifting up; it falls here like a held breath after the accusation.

philological_notes.note: 'To lift the face of': to show partiality, to give someone a favorable hearing because of who they are. Metzudat Zion links 'se'et' to flattery, citing Prov 18:5 'to lift the face of the wicked'. Radak: they favor the wicked because they are strong, great and rich, and do not take the poor man's case from their hands.
Injustice, wrong; from a root for being crooked. 'Judging injustice' is the exact opposite of 'doing justice' (mishpat).

verses.translation_literal: Judge the weak and fatherless; the afflicted and destitute declare righteous.
verses.translation_dramatic: Judge for the weak and the fatherless. Let the afflicted and the destitute hear the word they have waited for: you are in the right.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the voice of God turns from accusation to command, and the commands are short, almost clipped: 'shiftu... hatzdiku'. The two verbs form the frame. 'Shaphat' is to judge, 'hitzdik' is to declare someone 'tzaddik', in the right; in other words, to acquit. The KJV 'defend the poor' softens a verb that means 'give judgment for' and so loses the courtroom; 'do justice to the afflicted' likewise turns the declaration of innocence into a vague kindness. The four words for the weak, 'dal, yatom, 'ani, rash', are not a list of the pitiable; they are the people with no standing in the gate. The fatherless 'yatom' is one with no male protector, who in an agrarian clan society had no one to speak for him in the court at the city gate; the poor are the ones who cannot afford a bribe.

The commentators insist the command is about truth, not charity. Rashi on 'hatzdiku': if the poor man is in the right, do not overturn his case in order to favor the wicked. Radak likewise: when the right is with them, declare them in the right and do not fear their oppressors. Metzudat David adds a further turn: do not say, 'I will find for the rich man in this case, so as not to shame him', and only afterwards let it be known that the right was with his opponent.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil imperative: 'declare righteous, acquit, vindicate'. It is the forensic opposite of 'hirshi'a', 'declare guilty'. Rashi: if he is in the right in his case, do not overturn his case in order to favor the wicked.
A child without a father. In law codes the fatherless, the widow and the stranger are the standing trio of those God protects (Deut 10:18).

verses.translation_literal: Let the weak and needy escape; from the hand of the wicked snatch them away.
verses.translation_dramatic: Set the weak and the needy free. Reach in and pull them out of the wicked man's grip.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verbs have escalated from the courtroom into the street. In v. 3 the gods were to give judgment; here they are to let the poor 'escape' and 'rescue' them, the verbs of a man pulled from a fire or a flood. 'Paltu' is the language of the one who slips away from danger; 'hatzilu' is to snatch out. The 'hand of the wicked' is the actual physical grip of the oppressor, the creditor who seizes the field or the child. The KJV 'rid them out of the hand' is a Tudor idiom for freeing, now meaningless; the Hebrew is plain and violent.

Ibn Ezra splits the verse in two: judge the poor in the matter of their money, and rescue them in the matter of their life. Radak and Metzudat David keep it close to the case: save them from those who would rob them. It is a good note for the actor: the law's result is a body saved, not a paper verdict.

philological_notes.note: Piel imperative: 'cause to escape, deliver'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as rescue. Ibn Ezra reads the pair 'judge the poor with money, deliver the poor with life'.
'From the hand of the wicked': the hand is power, the grasp of the oppressor.

verses.translation_literal: They do not know and they do not understand; in darkness they walk about; shaken are all the foundations of the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: They do not know. They do not understand. They go stumbling on in the dark, and as they stumble the pillars beneath the earth begin to shake.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tone shifts from command to lament. It is like a prophet turning from the court to the audience and saying, quietly: they will not listen. Two verbs for knowing, 'yade'u... yavinu', hit like a tolling bell, and the word 'darkness' recalls the proverb in Exodus 23:8 that a bribe blinds the clear-sighted, as Rashi and Radak both observe. Hear the verb 'yithallekhu', 'they walk about', a reflexive form of habitual pacing: in the dark, with nowhere to go.

The last clause is the cosmic claim. 'Mosdei aretz', 'the foundations of the earth', are the pillars on which ancient people pictured the land set above the deep. The KJV 'out of course' is an astronomer's phrase that turns a collapsing building into a wandering star; the Hebrew verb 'yimotu' is simply 'they totter, they slip', the movement of something that is being loosed from its base. In the ancient world justice was not a social extra but a load-bearing wall: when judges give crooked verdicts the ordered world, the thing that stands against chaos, begins to give way. Radak and Meiri tie this to the Flood, when the earth was 'filled with violence' (Gen 6:11). Malbim says that without justice, men swallow each other alive.

philological_notes.note: 'The foundations of the earth', the cosmic pillars that hold the land above the waters; a standard image (Ps 18:16, Prov 8:29, Isa 24:18). They shake when justice fails.

Niphal of 'mot': to totter, slip, be shaken. It is the verb of Ps 15:5 ('he who does these things shall never be moved') and Ps 16:8, the opposite of stability; the ordered earth is now the thing that wobbles. KJV 'out of course' misses the physical sense.

verses.translation_literal: I, I said: gods are you, and sons of the Most High, all of you.
verses.translation_dramatic: I myself said it: you are gods. Sons of the Most High, every one of you.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the verse that made the psalm famous, and the actor must hold it very still. The pronoun 'ani' is separate and emphatic: 'I, even I, said it'. The speaker is reminding them that their rank is a gift, not a right: I called you gods. Notice the cadence: 'elohim attem' puts 'gods' first, ahead of 'you', and the second half, 'u-vene 'elyon kullekhem', 'and sons of the Most High, all of you', ends on 'all of you', a phrase that is both an honor and a net: no one is exempt from what follows in v. 7. The KJV 'children of the most High' is accurate enough as grammar but loses the family tie; 'bene' means sons, the members of a household. The title 'Most High', 'Elyon', is itself an old divine title (compare Gen 14:19).

The commentators take this in different ways. Rashi: those addressed (Israel, or its judges) were made like angels when they received the Torah, on condition that the Angel of Death would no longer rule over them. Radak and Meiri read it of judges, called gods when they judge truly; Malbim says judges are partners with God in sustaining the world. A reader today, following the divine council reading, hears something sharper: the beings called gods by the surrounding peoples are here made God's subordinates, his sons, and then judged. The verse is quoted by Jesus in John 10:34.

philological_notes.note: 'Gods are you': predicate before subject, so the stress falls on 'gods'. Rashi: angels; Radak and Meiri: judges, called gods when they judge truly.
'Sons of the Most High': members of the divine household or council. 'Elyon' is an old title of God. Ibn Ezra: 'like the angels'.

verses.translation_literal: Nevertheless, like a human being you will die, and like one of the princes you will fall.
verses.translation_dramatic: And yet. Like any man you will die. Like any prince, you will fall.
verses.directors_commentary:
The reversal of v. 6 lands in one word: 'akhen', 'nevertheless, yet truly'. The gods have been told they are sons of the Most High, and now they are told they will die as men do. 'Adam' here is humankind, the mortal creature of dust: the sting is that those who were called gods are sentenced to mortality, the one thing gods do not do. Rashi and Metzudat David hear the first Adam, who also lost his place through failing to keep the commandment. Radak reads it differently: their soul will die with the body, like any man's, and will not ascend with the sons of the Most High. The KJV 'ye shall die like men' is fair, but the Hebrew has the singular 'ke-adam', 'as the human', a collective, and the parallel 'ke-ehad ha-sarim', 'like one of the princes', is the part that makes the verse bite: the fall of the great is proverbially the hardest. The verb 'tipolu', 'you will fall', is the language of battle and of sudden ruin.

'Ha-sarim' has a double edge. On the human reading it means the earthly rulers whose fall is the common fate of tyrants; on the council reading it means the heavenly princes, and Rashi notes the aggadic link to Isaiah 24:21, where the Lord punishes the host of the heavens on high. Malbim says: the height from which they fall increases the fall.

philological_notes.note: 'Nevertheless, truly': an adverb of contrast and certainty. After 'you are gods' it turns the whole psalm.
'Like Adam / like a human you will die.' Rashi and Metzudat David hear the first man; Radak hears ordinary mortal humanity, with the soul dying alongside the body; the plain sense is mortal humanity.

verses.translation_literal: Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you will take as your possession among all the nations.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rise, O God, and judge the earth. For it is you who will hold all the nations as your own.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker changes. Everything since v. 1 was God's voice, and now the psalmist answers: 'qumah', 'rise up!', the old cry of prayer in the Psalms, used when God is asked to act (Ps 3:8, 7:7). Rashi hears Asaph praying that God rise and cut off the crooked judges from Israel. Play it small and urgent, after the long silence of the verdict. The verb 'shaphat' that opened the psalm returns, and now God alone is asked to judge, because the other judges have been sentenced.

The last clause is one of the hardest in the psalm. 'Tinchal be-khol ha-goyim' is literally 'you will inherit among all the nations'. The KJV 'thou shalt inherit all nations' smooths the 'be-' ('among, in') into a plain object, which is a choice. Ibn Ezra notes the problem and offers two solutions: the 'be-' is redundant, or, as Judah Halevi says, 'you will be an inheritance to the crying ones among all the nations'. On the council reading the verse is a quiet revolution: in Deuteronomy 32:8-9, in the reading of the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint (the Masoretic text has 'sons of Israel'), the nations were apportioned to the sons of God and Israel was the Lord's own portion; here the psalmist asks that the sentence on the failed gods be carried out and the nations become God's inheritance instead. Radak and Meiri read it differently, of the poor and oppressed of every nation, who are God's own portion.

philological_notes.note: 'Rise!': the call to God to act. The same verb opens Ps 3:8 and 7:7. It follows God's own standing (nitzav) in v. 1.

'You will inherit among all the nations.' Ibn Ezra explains the 'be-' as redundant, comparing 'Come, eat of (be-) my bread', or understands it with R. Judah Halevi as 'you will be the inheritance of those who cry out among all the nations'. Radak: you will take as your portion the oppressed in any people.
